query: Earlier studies of conventional metallic multilayers provide a general framework for deformation, but its conclusions may not transfer directly to high-entropy-alloy systems because compositional complexity, severe lattice distortion, and short-range order are associated with unusual deformation behavior. Preliminary evidence from FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers remains insufficient to establish what controls creep or when a given response dominates. Within the constraints of retaining a nanoscale multilayer coating and balancing strength with deformation tolerance, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading? State what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would expose it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, boundary conditions, relevant prior support, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Progressive plastic deformation (creep) in FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy (HEA) nanoscale multilayers under sustained loading is governed by the mobility of interfacial disconnections at semi-coherent FCC/BCC interfaces, which is controlled by the degree of chemical short-range order (SRO) and associated local compositional gradients at the interfaces. Higher interfacial SRO reduces pipe diffusion along misfit dislocations and raises the barrier for disconnection nucleation/climb, thereby suppressing time-dependent interfacial shear; reducing SRO has the opposite effect and promotes progressive deformation.
generation.material_initial_state: Alternating FCC/BCC HEA nanoscale multilayer coating (total thickness >1 µm; individual layer thickness 10–50 nm) with columnar grains and semi-coherent FCC/BCC interfaces; as-deposited interfaces are near-random solid solutions with modest interfacial misfit dislocation densities.
generation.intervention: Create otherwise identical multilayers that differ only in interfacial SRO: (i) increase SRO by low-temperature aging (below recrystallization, sufficient to develop local chemical order) or by interfacial compositional biasing during deposition; (ii) reduce SRO by rapid deposition/quenches or by inserting an ultrathin (<1 nm) interfacial dopant layer that frustrates local ordering. No changes to layer thickness, texture, or overall composition beyond the interface-local modification.
generation.conditions: Constant-load nanoindentation hold or micropillar compression creep at 25–300°C (≈0.2–0.4 Tm of the lowest-melting principal element), in inert atmosphere; sustained stresses below yield of the stronger BCC layer but above the threshold for time-dependent deformation; retain nanoscale layer thickness and semi-coherent interfaces.
generation.structural_mediator: Interfacial disconnections within the semi-coherent FCC/BCC interfaces, interacting with the misfit dislocation network that provides pipe-diffusion pathways; local SRO and compositional gradients at the interface modify core structure and diffusional kinetics of these defects.
generation.mechanism: Under sustained stress, creep proceeds via repeated nucleation, glide, and climb of interfacial disconnections that incrementally shear the interface and couple to confined dislocations in adjacent layers. Climb and chemical shuffling at the interface require atomic diffusion along misfit dislocations and within the interfacial plane. Increased interfacial SRO and lattice distortion reduce local diffusivity and increase the energy barrier for disconnection nucleation/climb, thereby lowering interfacial shear rate. Disrupting SRO increases disconnection mobility and pipe diffusion, raising creep rate.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to an as-deposited baseline with low-to-moderate SRO, interfaces with intentionally increased SRO will show: (a) a lower steady-state creep rate at a given stress and temperature (approximately 2–5× reduction, direction certain, magnitude approximate); (b) a higher apparent activation energy for creep and/or larger threshold stress for the onset of measurable time-dependent strain; (c) fewer or slower interfacial disconnection events in in-situ TEM mechanical testing. Conversely, interfaces with frustrated SRO will exhibit faster progressive deformation (approximately 2–5× increase in rate) and earlier onset of interfacial shear under the same conditions. Stress exponent may shift toward higher values if disconnection climb becomes rate-limiting with increased SRO; direction expected, magnitude uncertain.
generation.baseline: As-deposited FCC/BCC HEA multilayer with near-random interfacial chemistry and semi-coherent interfaces displays measurable time-dependent strain under sustained load at 25–300°C, attributed to interfacial shear mediated by disconnections with moderate mobility.
generation.boundary: Effect is strongest when: (i) layer thickness remains ≤50 nm and interfaces are semi-coherent; (ii) temperatures are below those that erase SRO (≈>0.5 Tm) or cause recrystallization/intermixing; (iii) grain boundaries are not the dominant creep path (columnar grains spanning the thickness). Differences should diminish at high temperatures that disorder SRO, at large layer thicknesses (>100 nm) where bulk dislocation processes dominate, or at very low stresses below threshold for interfacial disconnection activity.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the rate change (2–5×) is approximate and may depend on the specific HEA chemistries and the true extent of SRO; the stress exponent and activation energy shifts are directionally predicted but not precisely quantifiable without system-specific data. The extent to which HEAs exhibit reduced diffusion (“sluggish diffusion”) at interfaces is composition-dependent and could moderate the effect size.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of FCC/BCC HEA multilayers matched in layer thickness, texture, grain size, and overall composition: Set A with enhanced interfacial SRO (via controlled aging or interfacial compositional bias) and Set B with frustrated SRO (via rapid deposition or ultrathin interfacial dopant). Verify interfacial SRO differences using atom probe tomography (interfacial clustering/order parameters), diffuse scattering/PDF, or STEM-EELS/EDS mapping, and quantify misfit dislocation networks via HR-TEM. Perform constant-load nanoindentation creep holds and micropillar compression creep at multiple stresses and temperatures (25–300°C). Conduct in-situ TEM straining to directly observe interfacial disconnection nucleation/glide/climb in both sets.
measurements: Steady-state creep rate vs applied stress for both sets at fixed temperatures
Activation energy from Arrhenius plots of creep rate at fixed stress for both sets
Threshold stress for measurable creep (extrapolated from rate–stress curves)
Stress exponent n from log(creep rate) vs log(stress)
Frequency and velocity of interfacial disconnection events observed in in-situ TEM
Quantitative metrics of interfacial SRO (order parameter, clustering) and misfit dislocation density
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If Set A (higher SRO) does not exhibit a lower creep rate than Set B at the same stress and temperature, with differences less than 20% across multiple conditions despite confirmed higher SRO, or if activation energy/threshold stress and in-situ disconnection mobility do not shift in the predicted directions (higher barriers and lower mobility with higher SRO), the hypothesis is falsified. Additionally, if creep behavior is dominated by bulk dislocation glide/climb without correlation to interfacial SRO metrics, the hypothesis is falsified.
